source.title: Recognizing Dementia from Neuropsychological Tests with State Space Models
source.authors: Liming Wang; Saurabhchand Bhati; C. Karjadi; R. Au; James R. Glass

record.tranche_reason: The study reports how classification performance changes with model size and training-data scale in speech-based dementia assessment, a different setting from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures AUC, not held-out cross-entropy loss. It does not fit or test power laws, extrapolate from small runs, or optimize a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation. Its scaling experiments bear on V6; the other reported findings, including segment-duration comparisons, do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper builds a speech-based dementia classifier and reports AUC for two model sizes (29m, 48m) trained on 50–400 hours per class. It fits no power law, measures no pretraining loss and makes no extrapolation. Its 'scaling' is supervised task-data size against classification AUC, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or loss. With only two model sizes, a monotone AUC rise cannot show the power-law form that V5 needs. Kaplan et al. is cited only as an analogy ('aligns with recent scaling-law observations'). No version is tested; the finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Note that the paper's 'scalable' in the conclusion mainly means handling over 1,000 training hours and 6-minute inputs efficiently, not a fitted scaling law. The authors also report that the small model shows diminishing returns after 200 h/class.
record.recipe_differences: Speech dementia classifiers are evaluated by AUC across training-data and model-size settings; the study does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling trends vary by model size and class count; the small model shows diminishing returns after 200 hours per class, while the medium model continues improving beyond 400 hours per class.

fits_no_version.finding: In speech dementia classifiers, test AUC rises with supervised training hours (50–400 h/class). The 48m model keeps improving at 400 h, while the 29m model shows diminishing returns after 200 h. The 48m model scores higher than the 29m model at each data level. Values are figure-only, on a test set of 10 recordings per class, with no uncertainty reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-specific classification performance of supervised speech models improves monotonically with labelled training data and model size.

record.problems: The test set is small (10 recordings per class in the stated test split). Figure 2a does not provide tabulated AUC values, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted as findings on the tested version. Segment-duration comparisons and silence/speaker-role ablations were not extracted because they do not measure the scale relationships named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No comparison of model shapes at a fixed parameter count.
Speech setting, but no power-law form is fitted or checked; only two model sizes.
No downstream performance is related to pretraining scale or pretraining loss.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed. Supervised task-data scaling of AUC is not the downstream-from-pretraining predictability that V6 names, and no predictive relationship is fitted. The model-size gaps stated in Section IV-B (10% for 2-class, 7% for 3-class) are only partly consistent with Table II. The test set is tiny (10 recordings per class).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No predictions from small runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model size and training tokens is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Although the task uses speech, the study does not test whether a power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.

The study measures dementia-classification AUC in speech models, not language-model downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss. It reports scaling trends, but no fitted predictive relationship.
The study does not compare fitting choices, exponents, or departures from a fitted power law.

rows.note: The text says AUC increased steadily through 400 hours per class; it also reports diminishing returns after 200 hours per class.
rows.check: AUC versus supervised task-data hours for a speech classifier. This is not pretraining loss and not downstream-from-pretraining scaling, and no power law is fitted. Values are figure-only. The text also says this model shows diminishing returns after 200 h/class.

rows.subject: Demenba-medium
rows.operation_detail: Compared classification AUC across model sizes.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison for the Demenba classifiers but does not specify the segmentation condition for this difference.
rows.check: A two-point model-size comparison that also differs in architecture (DASS-small vs DASS-medium). The stated 10% 2-class gap does not match Table II, which shows 0.77→0.82 (VAD) and 0.85→0.87 (SD). The row value repeats the text and is inconsistent with the table.

rows.check: The stated 7% 3-class gap matches VAD in Table II (0.68→0.75) but not SD (0.81→0.83). It is a two-point size comparison with no scaling form, so it bears on no version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Demenba speech-classification models, tested across 2- and 3-class tasks and training-data amounts up to 400 hours per class
reader_labels.reason: AUC rises with training data for both model sizes and class settings, and the medium model has higher reported AUC than the small model; see r1-r6. The study does not establish a fitted or extrapolatable predictive law.
